learn.title: Floating Solar Farms on Water
learn.intro: Floating solar farms place panels on reservoirs, lakes, and canals, solving land scarcity while boosting efficiency through natural cooling. This innovation is key for water-rich regions aiming to scale solar without competing for farmland.
learn.c1_text: Covering water bodies cuts evaporation by up to 70%, saving precious water. Panels stay cooler on water, boosting output 5-15% compared to land-mounted systems. Think of it as panels enjoying a natural air-conditioning effect.
learn.c2_text: A 1 MW floating plant needs ~2 acres less land than ground-mounted. Platforms use HDPE floats and mooring systems designed for waves up to 1.5m. This opens reservoirs and quarry lakes for dual-use energy generation.
learn.c3_text: India targets 10 GW floating solar by 2030. NTPC Ramagundam's 100 MW plant is Asia's largest. With 11,500 MW potential on reservoirs, states like Kerala and Andhra Pradesh are fast-tracking tenders.
learn.stat4: India floating solar target: 10 GW by 2030

learn.title: Floating Offshore Wind Platforms
learn.intro: Floating offshore wind unlocks deep-water sites with stronger, steadier winds. Unlike fixed-bottom turbines, floating platforms can be deployed in waters over 60m deep, opening vast new ocean areas for clean power generation.
learn.c1_text: Spar-buoy, semi-submersible, and TLP platforms anchor to seabed with cables. Each suits different depths and wave conditions. Hywind Scotland (30 MW) uses a spar-buoy in 100m depth, proving commercial viability.
learn.c2_text: Wind speeds 20-40% higher offshore mean 50% more capacity factor. Floating turbines avoid seabed mining, reducing marine habitat disruption. A single 12 MW floating turbine can power ~16,000 homes annually.
learn.c3_text: India's 38 GW offshore wind potential lies off Tamil Nadu and Gujarat. The 1 GW Dhanushkodi project is in planning. Floating tech suits India's steep continental shelf drop-off beyond 50m depth.
learn.stat4: Capacity factor: 50%+ for offshore floating wind

learn.title: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP)
learn.intro: CSP uses thousands of mirrors to focus sunlight, generating heat that drives turbines. Unlike PV, CSP stores thermal energy cheaply, delivering electricity after sunset. This makes it a grid-stabilizing baseload renewable option.
learn.c1_text: Heliostats (mirrors) track the sun and reflect rays to a central tower receiver. Temperatures reach 565°C, heating molten salt. Think of it as using a magnifying glass to start a fire, scaled to stadium-size.
learn.c2_text: Molten salt stores heat at 565°C for 10+ hours, enabling 24/7 power. No battery needed. A 100 MW CSP plant with 10-hour storage can power 80,000 homes after dark. This dispatchability is CSP's superpower over PV.
learn.c3_text: India has 1.5 million MW CSP potential in Rajasthan and Gujarat. A 50 MW CSP plant with storage was commissioned at Pokhran. MNRE is reviving CSP with storage to complement solar PV's intermittency.

learn.title: Bifacial Solar Panels
learn.intro: Bifacial panels capture sunlight on both front and rear surfaces, boosting energy yield. They work best with reflective surfaces like white gravel or water, making them ideal for India's arid and water-body installations.
learn.c1_text: Rear side absorbs reflected and diffused light from ground/albedo. White surfaces reflect 80% vs dark soil's 20%. Mounting height of 1m+ maximizes rear yield. Think of it as panels with a second solar face.
learn.c2_text: Bifacial gains depend on albedo, tilt, and height. A 20% boost is typical with white gravel. Single-axis trackers add another 15-25%. Combined, total yield can jump 40% vs fixed monofacial panels.
learn.c3_text: Bhadla Solar Park (2.2 GW) uses bifacial modules. India's ALMM list now mandates bifacial for government projects. With 300+ sunny days, bifacial gains are highest in Rajasthan and Gujarat deserts.
learn.stat4: ALMM mandates bifacial for govt projects

learn.title: Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) in India
learn.intro: RPO mandates that DISCOMs procure a set percentage of their power from renewable sources. It's India's key policy lever to drive renewable adoption, but compliance gaps and payment delays remain major challenges.
learn.c1_text: Each state sets solar and non-solar RPO targets (e.g., 10-15% solar by 2022). DISCOMs must buy RE certificates or green power. Think of it as a renewable quota for electricity retailers, enforced by state SERCs.
learn.c2_text: Non-compliance attracts penalties of ₹1-5/kWh shortfall. Many DISCOMs miss targets due to financial stress and grid constraints. The REC mechanism lets deficit DISCOMs buy certificates from surplus producers to meet obligations.
learn.c3_text: Despite 500 GW RE target by 2030, many states lag RPO compliance. Tamil Nadu and Karnataka lead; some states below 5% solar RPO. DISCOM debt of ₹6 lakh crore hampers timely renewable procurement payments.

learn.title: Power Purchase Agreement (PPA)
learn.intro: A PPA is a long-term contract between a renewable generator and a buyer (DISCOM or corporate) that guarantees revenue for the project. It's the backbone of project financing, enabling banks to lend against stable cash flows.
learn.c1_text: A PPA locks in tariff, duration (15-25 years), and payment terms. The buyer commits to purchase all or part of generated power. Think of it as a rent guarantee for a landlord — it de-risks the investment for lenders.
learn.c2_text: Banks lend 70-80% of project cost based on PPA cash flows. Secured PPA with creditworthy buyer = lower interest. Solar PPAs in India average ₹2.5-3.5/kWh. Corporate PPAs are rising as companies seek 24/7 clean power.
learn.c3_text: SECI auctions award projects via PPA with DISCOMs. Corporate PPAs grew 3x since 2020. Google, Amazon, and Indian firms sign PPAs for 1-2 GW. ISTS charges and banking charges remain key negotiation points.
